title: The Body of All Buddhas Is But One Dharmakaya
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: The original text is from the Avatamsaka Sutra (80 fascicles), Chapter Ten, “The Bodhisattva’s Questions on Clear Understanding.”

inline.s: The original text is from the Avatamsaka Sutra (80 fascicles), Chapter Ten, “The Bodhisattva’s Questions on Clear Understanding.”
The central theme of this passage: All the Buddhas attain liberation through a single path; why then do their Buddha-lands and all their various matters appear so different?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Manjushri asked the Bodhisattva Xianshou, saying: Son of the Buddha, all the World-Honored Buddhas, only through a single path, attain liberation

How is it that now we see all the Buddha-lands, with all their various matters, differing in so many ways? That is to say: the worlds, the realms of sentient beings, the teachings that tame them, the life-spans, the lights, the supernatural powers, the assemblies, the modes of instruction, the abiding of the Dharma — each has its differences. There is no one who, without being endowed with all the Buddha-Dharma, attains Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.

[One-Vehicle teaching] The single teaching that alone can lead a person to Buddhahood.
[and so attain liberation] and so attain liberation from

the transformational birth-and-death. There are two kinds of birth-and-death: delimited birth-and-death and transformational birth-and-death. Those who have ended delimited birth-and-death escape the six realms of transmigration; those who have ended transformational birth-and-death fully realize the fruit of Buddhahood. [Delimited birth-and-death] For sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because their lives are limited by their wholesome and unwholesome karma, their life-spans are bounded and their bodies are delimited; hence their birth-and-death is called “delimited birth-and-death.” Those who have ended delimited birth-and-death are freed from transmigration and leave the three realms. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the three vehicles (bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats) have already cut off the delusions of views and thought and ended delimited birth-and-death. In the course of their cultivation, their deluded thoughts gradually perish while their realization grows; this transition from delusion to awakening differs in each stage. Moving from an earlier stage to a later one is like going through one birth-and-death, hence it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” Those who have ended transformational birth-and-death fully realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Xianshou replied in verse: For Manjushri the Dharma is ever thus; the Dharma King
has but one Dharma; all unhindered ones, through a single path, escape birth-and-death.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Xianshou replied in verse: Manjushri, the way by which all the Buddhas attain Buddhahood is none other than this (“the Dharma is ever thus”); while on the causal ground, they are all, through the One-Vehicle teaching, sovereign with respect to the Dharma, and through a single path emerge from transformational birth-and-death.
[Dharma King] The Buddha, being sovereign with respect to the Dharma
“I am the Dharma King, sovereign over the Dharma.”

[Causal ground] From the ground of the ordinary person, when one first arouses the mind to study Buddhism, up to the time just before fully realizing Buddhahood — this entire process is called the “causal ground.”
One sovereign over the Dharma. [Through a single path, escape birth-and-death] Here “birth-and-death” refers to transformational birth-and-death.

[Ten powers] The ten powers the Tathagata possesses: one, the power of knowledge of what is and is not the case; two, the power of knowledge of the karmic retribution of the three times; three, the power of knowledge of the various absorptions and samādhi liberations; four, the power of knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings; five, the power of knowledge of the various understandings; six, the power of knowledge of the various realms; seven, the power of knowledge of the paths that lead everywhere; eight, the power of the unobstructed divine eye; nine, the power of knowledge of past lives with the outflows extinguished; ten, the power of knowledge of the permanent eradication of habitual tendencies. [Fearlessness] Also called “having no fear.” The Buddha, when teaching among the great assembly, has the virtue of being calm and fearless. There are four kinds, called the four fearlessnesses. [Four fearlessnesses] One, fearlessness in regard to all-knowledge; two, fearlessness in regard to the extinction of outflows; three, fearlessness in declaring the obstacles to the path; four, fearlessness in declaring the path that puts an end to suffering.
The body of all the Buddhas is but one Dharmakaya”
is meant to say that the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three times share one Dharmakaya, rather than each having its own Dharmakaya.
“but one Dharmakaya, one mind, one wisdom; the powers and the fearlessnesses are likewise”

undifferentiated: the Dharmakaya is undifferentiated, and the mind, wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses are also undifferentiated. In Chinese, “one” can also be used to express “the same,” for example, of differing colors. The “one” in “one Dharmakaya” means that these Dharmakayas are mutually undifferentiated. This is similar in meaning to “mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are not three different things.”
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are not three different things” means: the ultimate nature of these three — mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — is

undifferentiated. Here “mind” refers to the self-nature (not the discriminating mind). And this ultimate nature is precisely the Dharmakaya. That is to say, the Dharmakaya of these three — mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — is
If “all the Buddhas share one Dharmakaya and share one mind, wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses,” then this is in fact a single Buddha; how can we still speak of “all the Buddhas”?

Moreover, if “all the Buddhas share one Dharmakaya,” then since they share one Dharmakaya, they are just one Buddha — what need is there to go on to say they “share one mind, wisdom, powers, and fearlessnesses”?

is the primal state of the self-nature. If “all the Buddhas share one Dharmakaya,” that would mean the Buddha and sentient beings (and sentient beings are future Buddhas) all share the same self-nature. Does that make sense? Śākyamuni Buddha returned the self-nature to its original nature and so became a Buddha; since we share the same self-nature as Śākyamuni Buddha, our self-nature would likewise have returned to its original nature, and we too would of course have become Buddhas. How could we still be sentient beings suffering in the five turbidities of the evil world? The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, that is a sentient being; when the self-nature awakens, that is the Buddha.”
this single self-nature shared by the Buddha and sentient beings — is it deluded or awakened?
From this we can see that taking
“The body of all the Buddhas is but one Dharmakaya”
to mean “all the Buddhas share one Dharmakaya” is mistaken.
Moreover, this is a fundamental error that would lead to an erroneous understanding of the entire Buddha-Dharma! The harm it does is extremely great.

[Bodhi] In Chinese, translated as “awakening”; this is the Buddha’s great wisdom. [Assembly] Refers to the ocean-assembly. [Ocean-assembly]

as the karma-actions of sentient beings differ, so the world they behold

Here “karma-action” refers to the shared karma (the common karmic causes) created by these sentient beings.

[Two kinds of karma] Shared karma and individual karma. Shared karma is the karmic cause that brings about a shared retribution, as mountains, rivers, and lands are common; individual karma is the karmic cause that brings about each one’s distinct retribution, as bodies differ and pleasure and pain differ, and so on.
The Buddha-lands and the Buddha-body, the assemblies and the speech — such Buddha-Dharma, sentient beings cannot see.

[Vow] A vow of resolve. Vows are of two kinds, the general vow and the particular vows,
the four great vows are the general vow, while, for example,

twelve vows are particular vows. [The four great vows] Though sentient beings are countless, I vow to save them all; though afflictions are inexhaustible, I vow to sever them all; though the Dharma-gates are measureless, I vow to learn them all; though the Buddha-way is unsurpassed, I vow to attain it.
According to the inclinations of sentient beings’ minds, and by the power of their karmic results, so they see differences — this is due to the Buddha’s awesome spiritual power.
[Karmic result] The pleasurable and painful retributions brought about by wholesome and unwholesome karmic causes.
The Buddha-lands have no distinction, neither aversion nor love; but following the minds of sentient beings, so their seeing differs.
